blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical security vulnerability in aircraft Instrument Landing Systems (ILS), a system that has been in use since 1932 and was never designed with cyber threats in mind. The paper demonstrates how modern software-defined radio (SDR) technology enables adversaries to spoof ILS signals, potentially causing aircraft to deviate from their correct landing paths. The author emphasizes the severity of this threat, noting that landing is the most dangerous phase of flight and that pilots rely entirely on ILS instruments, especially in low-visibility conditions. The paper introduces two attack models: the 'overshadow attack,' which overpowers legitimate signals with adversarial ones, and the 'single-tone attack,' which requires lower power but is less precise. Experiments using a flight simulator and aviation-grade ILS receivers confirm that these attacks can go undetected by pilots, even during critical landing procedures. The key insight is that ILS, a foundational aviation system, is now vulnerable to low-cost, practical cyber-physical attacks due to advances in SDR technology.
paper_title: Wireless attacks on aircraft instrument landing systems
paper_abstract: Modern aircraft heavily rely on several wireless technologies for communications, control, and navigation. Researchers demonstrated vulnerabilities in many aviation systems. However, the resilience of the aircraft landing systems to adversarial wireless attacks have not yet been studied in the open literature, despite their criticality and the increasing availability of low-cost software-defined radio (SDR) platforms. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of aircraft instrument landing systems (ILS) to wireless attacks. We show the feasibility of spoofing ILS radio signals using commerciallyavailable SDR, causing last-minute go around decisions, and even missing the landing zone in low-visibility scenarios. We demonstrate on aviation-grade ILS receivers that it is possible to fully and in fine-grain control the course deviation indicator as displayed by the ILS receiver, in real-time. We analyze the potential of both an overshadowing attack and a lower-power single-tone attack. In order to evaluate the complete attack, we develop a tightly-controlled closed-loop ILS spoofer that adjusts the adversary’s transmitted signals as a function of the aircraft GPS location, maintaining power and deviation consistent with the adversary’s target position, causing an undetected off-runway landing. We systematically evaluate the performance of the attack against an FAA certified flight-simulator (X-Plane)’s AI-based autoland feature and demonstrate systematic success rate with offset touchdowns of 18 meters to over 50 meters.
